questions.q: A 35-year-old male presents with a 3-week history of a painless penile ulcer with indurated edges and a clean base. Inguinal lymph nodes are enlarged but non-tender. Dark-field microscopy of the ulcer exudate shows motile spiral organisms. What is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose
questions.exp: This is primary syphilis (Hunterian chancre). Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose is the drug of choice for primary and secondary syphilis. Doxycycline is the alternative for penicillin-allergic patients.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman with well-defined erythematous scaly plaques on the scalp, elbows, and knees develops multiple small raindrop-like lesions all over the body 2 weeks after a sore throat. Which type of psoriasis has she developed?
questions.exp: Guttate psoriasis presents as multiple small (<1 cm) drop-shaped plaques triggered by streptococcal pharyngitis. It is common in young patients and accounts for ~2% of all psoriasis cases.

questions.q: A 45-year-old farmer from Tamil Nadu presents with painless swelling of the right foot with multiple discharging sinuses exuding black granules. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.exp: Black-grain eumycetoma is most commonly caused by Madurella mycetomatis. White-grain eumycetoma is caused by Pseudallescheria boydii. Actinomadura madurae causes actinomycetoma with white-yellow granules.

questions.q: A 10-year-old child presents with hypopigmented macules on the face with loss of sensation and a thickened greater auricular nerve. Slit-skin smear is negative. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.exp: Tuberculoid leprosy (paucibacillary) with negative slit-skin smear is treated with WHO MDT-PB: rifampicin 600 mg monthly (supervised) + dapsone 100 mg daily for 6 months.

questions.q: A 50-year-old male presents with tense blisters on erythematous skin affecting the trunk and flexures. Nikolsky sign is negative. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 at the dermoepidermal junction. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid presents with tense subepidermal blisters, negative Nikolsky sign, and eosinophilia. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 at the BMZ targeting BP180 (collagen XVII) and BP230. It is the most common autoimmune bullous disorder in the elderly.

questions.q: A 22-year-old HIV-positive man presents with multiple cauliflower-like perianal and penile lesions confirmed as condylomata acuminata by PCR. Which HPV types are most commonly responsible?
questions.exp: Condylomata acuminata (anogenital warts) are caused by low-risk HPV types 6 and 11 in >90% of cases. HPV 16 and 18 are high-risk types associated with cervical and anal carcinoma.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman on methotrexate for psoriasis develops erythema and erosions at sites of existing psoriatic plaques. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
questions.exp: Methotrexate-induced cutaneous ulceration at psoriatic plaques is a dose-related toxicity requiring immediate drug withdrawal. MTX preferentially affects rapidly dividing psoriatic keratinocytes, causing erosion/necrosis. Folinic acid rescue can be given after discontinuation.

questions.q: A 16-year-old boy presents with recurrent vesicles on the dorsa of hands after sun exposure, scarring, and milia. Urine turns reddish-brown on standing and shows red fluorescence under Wood's lamp. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Congenital erythropoietic porphyria (Gunther's disease) is an AR disorder (uroporphyrinogen III cosynthase deficiency) presenting in childhood with severe photosensitivity, blistering, scarring, hypertrichosis, and red urine with pink-red Wood's lamp fluorescence.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man has a pearly nodule with rolled borders, central ulceration, and telangiectasias on the nose tip. What is the most appropriate surgical treatment?
opts: Wide local excision with 5 mm margins
questions.exp: Nodular BCC on the nose (H-zone) is best managed with Mohs micrographic surgery (MMS), which provides the highest cure rate (99%) with maximal tissue conservation. MMS is indicated for H-zone tumours, morphoeic BCC, recurrent lesions, and large tumours.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman has bilateral malar brownish macules worsening in summer and after starting oral contraceptive pills. What is the first-line topical treatment for melasma?
questions.exp: Hydroquinone 4% cream (tyrosinase inhibitor) is the gold standard topical treatment for melasma. Modified Kligman's formula (hydroquinone 5% + tretinoin 0.1% + fluocinolone 0.01%) is used for resistant cases. Strict broad-spectrum sun protection is mandatory.

questions.q: A 6-year-old child has honey-colored crusted lesions around the nose and mouth. Culture grows MRSA. What is the treatment of choice?
questions.exp: Community-acquired MRSA impetigo requires systemic antibiotics. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (co-trimoxazole) is the first-line oral option for CA-MRSA skin infections. Topical mupirocin/fusidic acid are used for limited MSSA disease. Cefalexin is ineffective against MRSA.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman with SLE develops sclerodactyly and digital ulcers. ANA shows anti-Scl-70 antibodies. What is the most likely overlap diagnosis?
questions.exp: Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) is specific for diffuse SSc. Coexisting SLE features (ANA, oral ulcers, photosensitivity) with SSc features (sclerodactyly, digital ulcers, Raynaud's) and anti-Scl-70 defines lupus-scleroderma overlap syndrome.

questions.q: A 5-year-old boy has grouped vesicles on the right forehead and scalp with vesicles also on the tip of the nose. What does nasal tip involvement signify?
opts: Nasociliary nerve involvement — high risk of ocular complications
questions.exp: Hutchinson's sign — vesicles on the tip or side of the nose — indicates involvement of the nasociliary branch of V1, which also supplies the cornea. It predicts a high risk of herpes zoster ophthalmicus (keratitis, uveitis, visual loss) and mandates urgent ophthalmology referral.

questions.q: A patient with lepromatous leprosy on MDT develops sudden painful erythematous nodules on extremities and face with high fever. ESR is markedly elevated. What is the first-line treatment for this reaction?
questions.exp: Erythema nodosum leprosum (Type 2 lepra reaction) occurs in LL/BL leprosy and is TNF-α driven. Thalidomide is the drug of choice (100-400 mg/day), but is teratogenic and contraindicated in women of childbearing age. Prednisolone is used instead in women. MDT must be continued.

questions.q: A 19-year-old woman has moderate-severe acne unresponsive to 4 months of topical therapy. Which systemic drug requires two forms of contraception due to highest teratogenicity risk?
questions.exp: Oral isotretinoin (13-cis-retinoic acid) is the most teratogenic drug used in dermatology, causing craniofacial, cardiac, and CNS defects. Two reliable contraceptive methods are mandatory from 1 month before to 1 month after treatment. It targets all four pathogenic mechanisms of acne.

questions.q: A 42-year-old man has pruritic grouped vesicles on elbows, knees, and buttocks. DIF shows granular IgA at the BMZ. What systemic condition is most strongly associated?
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (Duhring's disease) is pathognomically associated with celiac disease in >85% of patients. Granular IgA at papillary dermis on DIF is pathognomonic. Treatment: dapsone (rapid symptom relief) + strict gluten-free diet (disease control and cancer prevention).

questions.q: A 65-year-old male smoker develops a rapidly growing keratotic nodule with a central keratin-filled crater on the cheek over 6 weeks. Biopsy shows well-differentiated squamous epithelium with a crater-like architecture. What is this lesion?
questions.exp: Keratoacanthoma (KA) is a rapidly growing, potentially self-resolving lesion with a central keratin-filled crater on sun-exposed skin. It is regarded by many as a well-differentiated SCC variant and is best treated by excision. Rapid growth distinguishes it from typical SCC.

questions.q: A newborn presents with generalized flaccid blisters at birth. The mother has untreated pemphigus vulgaris. What is the mechanism of neonatal blistering?
opts: Passive transplacental transfer of maternal IgG anti-desmoglein antibodies
De novo autoimmune response in the neonate
questions.exp: Neonatal pemphigus results from passive transplacental transfer of maternal IgG anti-desmoglein 1 and/or 3 antibodies. It typically resolves within 4-6 weeks as maternal antibodies are cleared. Management is supportive; systemic steroids are rarely required.

questions.q: A 38-year-old woman has violaceous papules on wrists and ankles with a lacy white oral mucosal pattern. Biopsy shows band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at DEJ, saw-tooth rete ridges, and Civatte bodies. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Lichen planus presents with the 6 P's: Pruritic, Planar, Polygonal, Purple Papules and Plaques. Wickham's striae (lacy white) are characteristic. Histology shows band-like T-cell infiltrate, saw-tooth rete ridges, and Civatte bodies (apoptotic keratinocytes at DEJ). Oral LP is potentially premalignant.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman has progressive tightening of facial skin, loss of oral aperture, and Raynaud's phenomenon. ANA shows anti-centromere antibodies. What type of systemic sclerosis does she have?
questions.exp: Anti-centromere antibodies are specific for limited cutaneous SSc (CREST: Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia). Skin involvement is limited to distal extremities and face. Anti-Scl-70 is associated with diffuse cutaneous SSc.

questions.q: A 28-year-old man presents with perifollicular haemorrhagic papules, corkscrew hairs, and gingival bleeding after 6 months of dietary restriction. What is the underlying deficiency?
questions.exp: Scurvy (vitamin C deficiency) presents with perifollicular haemorrhage, corkscrew/swan-neck hairs, gingival bleeding, and poor wound healing due to defective collagen synthesis (ascorbate is required for proline/lysine hydroxylation). Treatment is ascorbic acid supplementation.

questions.q: A 45-year-old HIV-positive man has painful red-violet plaques and nodules on the lower extremities. Biopsy shows spindle cells, vascular slits, and HHV-8 positive staining. What is the preferred first-line systemic treatment for advanced disease?
questions.exp: Epidemic (AIDS-associated) Kaposi's sarcoma is caused by HHV-8. Pegylated liposomal doxorubicin is the preferred first-line chemotherapy for advanced/disseminated KS (response rate ~60%). HAART is also essential. Interferon-alpha is used in classic KS with preserved immune function.

questions.q: A 30-year-old male has a well-defined, raised, oval plaque with a lilac/violaceous border and ivory-white center on the trunk without Raynaud's or systemic symptoms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Morphea presents as indurated plaques with an ivory/white center and lilac/violaceous inflammatory border ('lilac ring'). It is limited to the skin without systemic involvement, unlike SSc. Treatment includes topical/intralesional steroids, calcipotriol, and UVA1 phototherapy.

questions.q: A 7-year-old child from Bihar has marked photosensitivity, ataxia, and pellagra-like rash. Urine amino acid chromatography shows neutral aminoaciduria. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Hartnup disease is an AR disorder of neutral amino acid transport (SLC6A19 mutation). Impaired tryptophan intestinal absorption reduces niacin synthesis, causing pellagra-like photosensitive rash, cerebellar ataxia, and psychiatric symptoms. Neutral aminoaciduria is diagnostic. Treatment: nicotinamide supplementation.

questions.q: A 33-year-old woman undergoes patch testing for suspected contact dermatitis. The test site shows erythema, edema, and vesicles (++ reaction) at 48 hours that intensifies at 96 hours. What type of hypersensitivity reaction underlies this?
questions.exp: Allergic contact dermatitis is a Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity mediated by sensitized CD4+ Th1 and CD8+ cytotoxic T cells. The reaction peaks at 48-96 hours. Langerhans cells are the primary antigen-presenting cells during the sensitization phase.

questions.q: A 50-year-old man has recurrent oral erosions and flaccid blisters on normal-appearing skin. DIF shows intercellular IgG in a 'chicken-wire' pattern. The biopsy shows suprabasal acantholysis. What is the primary autoantigen targeted?
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris with mucosal-predominant disease targets desmoglein 3 (highly expressed in oral mucosa). Mucocutaneous PV has both anti-Dsg1 and anti-Dsg3 antibodies. Pemphigus foliaceus targets only Dsg1. DIF shows intercellular IgG throughout the epidermis in a net/chicken-wire pattern.

questions.q: A 42-year-old woman with Indian skin phototype IV wants permanent reduction of dark terminal hair on her upper lip. Which laser is safest and most appropriate?
questions.exp: Nd:YAG 1064 nm laser is safest for Fitzpatrick skin phototypes IV-VI. Its longer wavelength has relatively less epidermal melanin absorption, reducing the risk of burns and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation in dark skin. Ruby and alexandrite lasers carry higher risk of epidermal damage in pigmented skin.

questions.q: A 24-year-old woman has violaceous nodules and plaques on the nose and cheeks with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and elevated ACE levels. Biopsy shows non-caseating granulomas. What is this specific cutaneous pattern called?
questions.exp: Lupus pernio is a specific form of cutaneous sarcoidosis presenting as violaceous indurated plaques on the nose, cheeks, and ears. It strongly correlates with chronic systemic sarcoidosis (pulmonary fibrosis, bone, and eye involvement). Despite the name, it is unrelated to lupus erythematosus.

questions.q: A 20-year-old medical student develops erythema, scaling, and fissuring in the web spaces between fingers after starting clinical rotations, worsening with repeated hand washing. Patch test to standard series is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Irritant contact dermatitis (ICD) from repeated exposure to detergents/water is the most common occupational skin disease among healthcare workers. Unlike allergic CD, patch testing is negative. Management: barrier protection, emollients, moisturizing soaps, and topical corticosteroids for active inflammation.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman on long-term hydrochlorothiazide develops blisters on sun-exposed skin of the forearms and dorsal hands. DIF shows IgG at the BMZ. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Pseudoporphyria is a drug-induced blistering disorder mimicking PCT clinically (fragile skin, blisters on sun-exposed areas, milia) but without porphyrin abnormalities. NSAIDs, nalidixic acid, furosemide, and thiazide diuretics are classic causative drugs. DIF may show IgG/C3 at BMZ.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child presents with erosions around the mouth, nose, and eyes along with perianal skin redness, diarrhea, and alopecia. Serum zinc is markedly low. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Acrodermatitis enteropathica is an AR disorder of zinc absorption (SLC39A4/ZIP4 transporter mutation) presenting with the triad of acral and periorificial dermatitis, alopecia, and diarrhea. It typically manifests after weaning from breast milk. Treatment: lifelong oral zinc supplementation. Dramatic response occurs within days.
